title: How do you test Spring Kafka — `@EmbeddedKafka` / `EmbeddedKafkaBroker` for integration tests against an in-memory broker (or Testcontainers for a real one), how do you write a producer+consumer integration test, and how do you mock `KafkaTemplate` in a pure unit test?
shortTitle: How do you test Spring Kafka — embedded broker integration tests and mocking KafkaTemplate in unit tests?

s1_definition.profdef: Spring Kafka offers two layers of testing. For integration tests you run against a real broker without external infrastructure: `@EmbeddedKafka` starts an in-memory Kafka broker inside the test JVM exposed as an `EmbeddedKafkaBroker`, or Testcontainers starts a genuine Kafka container in Docker for higher fidelity. You use these to verify end-to-end that a producer publishes and a consumer actually receives and processes. For pure unit tests you do not start any broker; you mock `KafkaTemplate` with a mocking framework and assert that your code called `send` with the right topic, key, and value, keeping the test fast and focused on logic.
s1_definition.analogy: Testing Spring Kafka at National Bank of India is like rehearsing the mailroom in two ways. A unit test is a dry run where you hand the clerk a fake mailbox and just check that they addressed the envelope correctly, without actually mailing anything; it is instant and only checks the clerk's logic. An integration test is a full rehearsal with a small practice post office set up inside the building, the embedded broker, where you genuinely drop the letter in and confirm the person at the other counter receives and opens it. Testcontainers is the same rehearsal but using a real miniature post office spun up just for the test, which behaves exactly like the real one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Mock KafkaTemplate for fast unit tests of your logic, and use an embedded broker or Testcontainers for integration tests that prove a producer and consumer really work end to end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spring Kafka offers two layers of testing. For integration tests you run against a real broker without external infrastructure: `@EmbeddedKafka` starts an in-memory Kafka broker inside the test JVM exposed as an `EmbeddedKafkaBroker`, or Testcontainers starts a genuine Kafka container in Docker for higher fidelity. You use these to verify end-to-end that a producer publishes and a consumer actually receives and processes. For pure unit tests you do not start any broker; you mock `KafkaTemplate` with a mocking framework and assert that your code called `send` with the right topic, key, and value, keeping the test fast and focused on logic.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Testing Spring Kafka at National Bank of India is like rehearsing the mailroom in two ways. A unit test is a dry run where you hand the clerk a fake mailbox and just check that they addressed the envelope correctly, without actually mailing anything; it is instant and only checks the clerk's logic. An integration test is a full rehearsal with a small practice post office set up inside the building, the embedded broker, where you genuinely drop the letter in and confirm the person at the other counter receives and opens it. Testcontainers is the same rehearsal but using a real miniature post office spun up just for the test, which behaves exactly like the real one.

**One line to remember:** Mock KafkaTemplate for fast unit tests of your logic, and use an embedded broker or Testcontainers for integration tests that prove a producer and consumer really work end to end.

sections.s2_technical:
A pure unit test should never touch a broker, because starting Kafka is slow and brings infrastructure concerns into a test that is only meant to check your business logic. Instead you mock the `KafkaTemplate`. With a mocking framework you create a mock template, inject it into the class under test, call the method, and then verify the interaction, for example `verify(kafkaTemplate).send("transfer.completed", "SAV2001", expectedEvent)`. If your code depends on the returned future, you stub it to return a completed future so the code under test proceeds, for example `when(template.send(any(), any(), any())).thenReturn(CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null))`. This keeps the test in milliseconds and isolated, and it is the right level to check that, say, the service builds the correct event and publishes it to the correct topic and key.

An integration test verifies the real wiring: serialization, partitioning, the listener container, offset commits, and error handling. `@EmbeddedKafka` on a test class boots an in-memory broker in the same JVM, and Spring injects an `EmbeddedKafkaBroker` you can use to configure producers and consumers. You set the test's bootstrap servers to the embedded broker's address, usually with `@EmbeddedKafka(partitions = 1, topics = "transfer.completed")` and a property that points the application context at `${spring.embedded.kafka.brokers}`. You then produce a record through a real KafkaTemplate and assert that your real consumer processed it, or you build a test consumer to read the output topic and assert the record arrived.

Writing the producer plus consumer integration test has a timing subtlety: consumption is asynchronous, so the test must wait for the record to be received rather than asserting immediately. The common patterns are to use a `CountDownLatch` that the listener counts down when it receives the record and then `latch.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`, or to use the `Consumer` created from `KafkaTestUtils` and call `KafkaTestUtils.getSingleRecord(consumer, "topic")` which blocks until a record is available. You also use awaitility or a polling assertion to wait for a side effect, such as a row appearing in the database, because the listener runs on its own thread. The key discipline is to synchronise on the actual completion signal, never to use a fixed sleep, which is flaky.

Testcontainers is the higher-fidelity option: instead of the embedded in-JVM broker, it starts a real Kafka container in Docker for the duration of the test, so you are testing against the exact broker version you run in production, including real networking and real broker behaviour that the embedded broker sometimes simplifies. You use a `KafkaContainer`, start it, and point the bootstrap servers at `container.getBootstrapServers()`. The senior nuances are that embedded Kafka is faster and needs no Docker so it is ideal for the bulk of integration tests, while Testcontainers is slower but worth it for tests that depend on precise broker semantics or exact version compatibility; that you should keep unit tests the majority and integration tests a smaller, focused set because the broker-backed tests are heavier; that you must clean up consumer groups and use unique group ids or random ports to avoid cross-test interference; and that testing error paths, like a poison pill routing to a dead letter topic, is best done as an integration test because that behaviour lives in the container and serialization layer, not in your business method.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that the transfer-event publishing and the settlement consumer kept breaking in subtle ways that unit tests alone never caught, and the team needed a reliable testing strategy.

Problem 1 — a junior changed the topic name in the service and all the unit tests still passed because they never checked the actual topic, so the regression reached staging. This is exactly what a mocked KafkaTemplate unit test prevents: assert that the service calls send with the exact topic and key, catching the mistake instantly without any broker.

Problem 2 — serialization and the listener wiring broke once when a field type changed, and no unit test could see it because mocks never serialize. This is exactly what an embedded-broker integration test catches: publish a real event and assert the real consumer deserializes and settles it end to end.

Problem 3 — a production incident came from behaviour that only the real broker version exhibited, and the embedded broker had masked it. This is exactly what Testcontainers addresses: run the critical path against the real broker image used in production.

The code will show a `TransferEventPublisher` unit-tested with a mocked template asserting the topic and key, and a settlement flow integration-tested with an embedded broker using a latch to wait for asynchronous consumption. Because the required demo must be runnable, the main demo models the two testing styles with a fake template that records calls and an in-JVM broker stand-in with a latch, so you can see both a unit-style assertion and an integration-style end-to-end receive. The demo step is: run the unit-style check that verifies the publish call, then run the integration-style flow that publishes and waits for the consumer to receive and settle.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the demo
javac com/bank/transfer/demo/TestingStylesDemo.java
java com.bank.transfer.demo.TestingStylesDemo

# In a real Spring Boot project
mvn test                       # runs unit + @EmbeddedKafka integration tests
mvn -Dtest=SettlementIntegrationTest test
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a transfer for Rajesh, exercised first through the unit-test style and then through the integration-test style.

Step 1: In the unit-test style, a mocked KafkaTemplate is injected into the publisher. The publisher builds the TransferEvent and calls send with topic transfer.completed and key SAV2001. No broker is involved and nothing is serialized.

Step 2: The test asserts the interaction: it checks that send was called with exactly that topic and key. The mock recorded the call, so the assertion passes, and this would have failed instantly if a junior had changed the topic name.

Step 3: In the integration-test style, an embedded in-JVM broker starts and the settlement listener subscribes to transfer.completed, holding a countdown latch.

Step 4: A real template publishes the TransferEvent to the embedded broker. The broker delivers it asynchronously on a separate thread, exactly like a real listener container, so the data genuinely flows through serialize, broker, and deserialize.

Step 5: The listener receives the event, settles it, and counts down the latch. The test waits on the latch with a timeout rather than a fixed sleep, so it proceeds the moment consumption happens.

Step 6: The latch reaches zero within the timeout, proving end-to-end delivery. The output shows the unit-style verification passing and the integration-style consumer receiving and settling the event.

```
2026-10-24 23:10:02 [INFO] === UNIT TEST style: mock template, assert the send call ===
2026-10-24 23:10:02 [INFO] verify send(topic,key) matched = true
2026-10-24 23:10:02 [INFO] === INTEGRATION TEST style: embedded broker + latch, end to end ===
2026-10-24 23:10:02 [INFO] settled txn=TXN-1 account=SAV2001 amount=Rs.50000
2026-10-24 23:10:02 [INFO] consumer received end-to-end = true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  UNIT TEST (fast, no broker)
    TransferEventPublisher.publish("SAV2001", 50000)
        │ template.send("transfer.completed","SAV2001",event)
        ▼
    MockKafkaTemplate records the call
        │
        ▼
    verify send(topic,key) == expected  (milliseconds)

  INTEGRATION TEST (@EmbeddedKafka, real wiring)
    RealKafkaTemplate.send(...)
        │ serialize + publish
        ▼
    EmbeddedBroker (in-JVM) → async delivery on listener thread
        │
        ▼
    SettlementListener.onEvent() → settle → latch.countDown()
        │
        ▼
    test: latch.await(5s) == true  (end-to-end proven)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I test Spring Kafka at two levels, and I keep them clearly separated. For pure unit tests I never start a broker, because that is slow and pulls infrastructure into a test that should only check logic. Instead I mock the KafkaTemplate, inject it into the class under test, call the method, and verify that it called send with exactly the right topic, key, and value, stubbing the returned future as already completed if the code needs it. This runs in milliseconds and catches logic mistakes instantly, for example a topic name being changed by accident.

For integration tests I run against a real broker so I exercise the parts that mocks cannot, namely serialization, partitioning, the listener container, offset commits, and error handling. The lightweight option is the embedded Kafka broker, which starts an in-memory broker inside the test JVM and gives me an embedded broker handle; I point the context's bootstrap servers at it, publish a real event with a real template, and assert the real consumer received and processed it. The important detail is that consumption is asynchronous, so I synchronise on the actual completion signal, typically a countdown latch that the listener triggers on receive, or a blocking read from the test utilities, and I never use a fixed sleep because that is flaky.

When I need the highest fidelity I use Testcontainers, which spins up a genuine Kafka container in Docker matching the exact broker version we run in production. It is slower than the embedded broker, but it is the right choice for the critical paths and for anything that depends on precise broker semantics that the embedded broker sometimes simplifies.

In the transfer service at National Bank of India this strategy paid off directly. A mocked-template unit test caught a change to the transfer topic name before it ever left a developer's machine, an embedded-broker test caught a serialization break when a field type changed on the TransferEvent, and a Testcontainers test on the settlement path reproduced a broker-version-specific behaviour that the embedded broker had been hiding. The senior nuance I always add is to keep unit tests the majority for speed and focus, use a smaller focused set of broker-backed integration tests, give each test a unique consumer group or random port to avoid cross-test interference, and test error paths like poison-pill-to-dead-letter-topic as integration tests, because that behaviour lives in the serialization and container layers, not in the business method.
